How performant is our tiff ex port?

About **2–3 seconds per 20–24 MP photo on the headless A4000**:

| Image | TIFF export | File size |
|---|---:|---:|
| 20 MP RAW | 2.0–2.3 s | 121 MB |
| 24 MP RAW | 2.2–2.7 s | 146 MB |

Those timings include RAW decoding, GPU rendering, readback, compression, and writing the TIFF. **Complete Finish adds cache writes, hashing, and publication**, which I haven’t separately benchmarked.

We reuse the saved BPAM adjustments—no inference during export. Compression runs across CPU cores; independent photos run concurrently within the GPU memory budget.

The clearest optimization opportunity is **file size and disk traffic**: these noisy samples compressed poorly. Exporting onto your slow HDD could cost substantially more than the rendering itself.
What is state of the art here? And that seems extremely large for a 24 megapixel image. Are we not doing any compression?
I’ll check the TIFF compression we’re using and compare it with current options, including what Lightroom supports.

**We are compressing, but poorly.** I checked: we use fast ZIP/Deflate on raw pixel bytes, **without TIFF’s horizontal predictor**. That’s an optimization I missed; blaming noise alone was premature.

The uncompressed arithmetic explains the size:

**24 million pixels × 3 channels × 2 bytes = 144 MB.**

So our ~146 MB output is effectively uncompressed. A camera RAW usually stores one sensor sample per pixel; a developed RGB16 image stores three.

For our workflow, the strongest options are:

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **TIFF + horizontal prediction + optimized Deflate** | Best straightforward improvement. Prediction losslessly stores differences between neighboring samples before compression. Benchmark `libdeflate` for speed and compression level. [Predictor documentation](https://gdal.org/en/stable/drivers/raster/gtiff.html), [libdeflate](https://github.com/ebiggers/libdeflate). |
| **Lossless JPEG XL** | The modern alternative I’d benchmark for smaller photographic files. Current Lightroom supports importing JXL and exporting lossless, 16-bit JXL. We’d still verify metadata and your complete import workflow. [Adobe format support](https://helpx.adobe.com/lightroom-classic/help/supported-file-formats.html), [export options](https://helpx.adobe.com/lightroom-classic/help/export-files-disk-or-cd.html). |

**My recommendation:** benchmark properly compressed TIFF against lossless JXL on the same rendered pixels. Keep every bit initially, and measure file size, encoding time, and Lightroom loading. We shouldn’t accept 146 MB as the optimized result—or promise a reduction before measuring it.

Great, please check 20 random-ish photographs from D:\Photos\Originals I say random-ish because fully random would require enumerating all of them, and I don't want to do that because the drive is on spinning rust. Test both optimized TIFF and JPEG XL.

All 160 encode/decode checks passed with exact pixel matches. Across the 20 photos, optimized TIFF saved 13.4%, fast lossless JPEG XL saved 20.7%, and higher-effort JPEG XL saved 25.3% versus our current TIFFs. Typical compression times were about 0.13 s, 0.47 s, and 1.30 s respectively; those exclude rendering and disk I/O.

Sony’s compressed RAW is a useful reference. I’ll check its tradeoff and how closely we can match it for developed images; compression of sensor data and compression of rendered RGB behave differently.

The closest practical analogue is **high-quality lossy JPEG XL**: allow small pixel changes to save much more space. There’s no exact setting equivalent to Sony’s RAW compression, since our export already contains developed RGB.

I’ll add JXL distances 0.5 and 1.0 to this benchmark. Libjxl describes 1.0 as “visually lossless”; 0.5 is more conservative. That makes a sensible candidate for an optional **Compact** export, with exact lossless still available. ([libjxl documentation](https://libjxl.github.io/libjxl/api_encoder.html))

The lossy settings are producing much smaller files: the first ten photos are generally in the single-digit to tens-of-megabytes range. This is the tradeoff you were pointing at. I’m keeping the quality claim separate from the size result: these files intentionally change pixels, and the codec’s “visually lossless” label doesn’t guarantee identical results after strong Lightroom edits.

The compact comparison is complete. At distance 0.5, median size fell to **11.7 MB**, versus **128.7 MB** for optimized TIFF and **111.3 MB** for higher-effort lossless JXL. Compression took about **0.65 seconds** per photo.

I’d use distance 0.5 as the starting point for an optional Compact mode. In the crops I checked, distance 1 smoothed grain more noticeably, so I wouldn’t choose it as the initial setting.

Yes—**high-quality lossy JPEG XL is the practical analogue**.

Sony’s traditional compressed RAW sacrifices some precision for smaller files. It also stores one sensor sample per pixel; our RGB16 export stores three 16-bit channels, which explains much of the size difference. [Technical analysis](https://library.imaging.org/admin/apis/public/api/ist/website/downloadArticle/ei/28/2/art00020)

I extended the benchmark to test that tradeoff on the **same 20 photographs**:

| Export | Median size | Encode time |
|---|---:|---:|
| Current TIFF | 148.2 MB | — |
| Optimized TIFF | 128.7 MB | 0.13 s |
| Lossless JXL, fast | 116.2 MB | 0.47 s |
| Lossless JXL, higher effort | 111.3 MB | 1.30 s |
| **Compact JXL, distance 0.5** | **11.7 MB** | **0.65 s** |
| Compact JXL, distance 1 | 7.0 MB | 1.08 s |

These are CPU compression times, excluding rendering and disk I/O. All lossless outputs matched exactly.

**I recommend an optional “Compact — high-quality JPEG XL” setting using distance 0.5**, alongside lossless output. Libjxl calls distance 1 “visually lossless”; 0.5 is more conservative. In the crops I checked, distance 1 smoothed grain more noticeably. Neither setting has an exact Sony-quality equivalent or guarantees unchanged appearance after aggressive editing. [Codec documentation](https://libjxl.github.io/libjxl/api_encoder.html)

The benchmark and results are committed and pushed. Production export settings are unchanged; Compact is now a measured candidate for integration.

My vote: **keep A; evaluate owning denoise without committing to this particular model.**

1. **Own denoise:** best eventual experience. Another 5–10× means roughly **1–2 seconds per 24 MP photo**. That might require a smaller model or substantially different inference implementation; I wouldn’t promise it from tuning this graph. 2. **Revert A:** sacrifices the feature you actually want because another component is unfinished. I wouldn’t choose this yet.

3. **Denoise JXL later in LR:** unfortunately, **Adobe explicitly excludes JXL from AI Denoise**, including lossless JXL. This is a format-support problem before it’s a quality problem. [Adobe documentation](https://helpx.adobe.com/lightroom/desktop/edit-photos/enhance-details.html)

4. **Reverse the handoff:** RAW → Adobe denoise → denoised linear DNG → **our A/HDR** → JXL. That preserves our rendering while outsourcing denoising. We’d need to qualify Adobe’s DNG handoff and our decoding; it’s a candidate workflow, not something currently working. More cumbersome, but potentially a useful escape hatch for important photos.

I’d judge these concert samples first. If the quality disappoints, change denoisers before investing heavily in speeding this one up.
